skill.name: ai-maestro-code-graph-query
skill.description: Query an AI Maestro code graph to inspect dependencies, callers, callees, associations, serializers, and related components before changing code.
skill.summary: Use AI Maestro graph queries to understand code relationships before editing.
skill.author: 23blocks-OS

security_audit.summary: The skill provides useful AI Maestro code graph workflows, but it relies on Bash execution and strongly mandates automatic graph queries after reading files. The highest risks are unbundled PATH-resolved scripts, hidden home-directory installation under ~/.local/bin, and coercive prompt text that can push agents to execute commands without fresh user intent.

remediation.issue: Automatic Bash execution is mandated by prompt text.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit user confirmation before running graph scripts, especially after file reads or searches.

remediation.issue: Graph scripts are not included in the reviewed skill package.
remediation.suggestion: Bundle the scripts or pin their absolute paths and checksums so reviewers can verify executed code.

remediation.issue: Installation targets ~/.local/bin and relies on PATH lookup.
remediation.suggestion: Avoid hidden home-directory installs, or document the path clearly and verify script ownership before execution.

remediation.issue: The skill uses curl to contact a localhost service.
remediation.suggestion: Disclose the local API dependency and avoid sending code content unless the user authorizes it.

semantic_findings.title: Prompt Injection Attempt Detected
semantic_findings.description: The skill uses forceful authority language such as "THIS IS NOT OPTIONAL" and requires immediate graph queries after every Read. This can override normal user intent and push automatic Bash execution.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text explicitly claims default authority over agent behavior and mandates tool use. It does not request data theft, so high severity is appropriate rather than critical.

semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command list and install guidance clearly rely on external shell scripts not present in the scanned files. This is a strong supply-chain and PATH-hijack risk.

content.value_statement: Changing code without dependency context can break callers, serializers, and related components. This skill uses AI Maestro graph commands to inspect relationships before edits.
actual_capabilities: Describe code components or functions through AI Maestro graph queries.
Find callers and callees for a function before changes.
Find serializers and model associations for data model updates.
Find related classes, modules, and components by relationship type.
Trace call paths between two named functions.
Run delta indexing to refresh changed project files.
limitations: Requires AI Maestro and its local API to be running on the workstation.
Requires graph scripts to be installed and available on PATH.
Requires an indexed project before queries return useful results.
Uses Bash commands, so users should review commands before execution.

use_cases.title: Review Model Change Impact
use_cases.description: Find serializers, associations, and dependent code before changing a model.

use_cases.title: Prepare Safer Refactors
use_cases.description: Identify callers and callees before changing a function signature or moving logic.

use_cases.title: Explore Unknown Codebases
use_cases.description: Map relationships between controllers, services, jobs, and components during onboarding.

prompt_templates.title: Inspect One Component
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the code graph to describe this component. Summarize what it depends on and what depends on it.

prompt_templates.title: Check Function Impact
prompt_templates.prompt: Find callers and callees for this function. Explain which callers need review before I edit it.

prompt_templates.title: Review Model Dependencies
prompt_templates.prompt: Find serializers, associations, and related components for this model. Highlight any risky downstream dependencies.

prompt_templates.title: Trace Cross-Layer Flow
prompt_templates.prompt: Trace the call path between this entry point and this internal function. Explain the main layers and change risks.

output_examples.input: Find the impact of changing the payment processing function.
output: The function is called by checkout, subscription renewal, and refund workflows.
It calls validation, card charging, and transaction logging logic.
Review checkout and renewal tests before changing the function signature.

output_examples.input: Check dependencies for the user model before adding a field.
output: The model has serializers for public profile and admin views.
It is associated with accounts, sessions, orders, and audit records.
Update serializer coverage and migration tests before exposing the new field.

best_practices: Confirm graph commands with the user before running Bash in a repository.
Refresh the graph index after meaningful code changes.
Compare graph results with tests before making high-impact refactors.
anti_patterns: Running PATH-resolved graph scripts without checking their source.
Treating graph output as complete when the index may be stale.
Changing public functions without reviewing callers and tests.

faq.question: What does this skill connect to?
faq.answer: It expects AI Maestro to expose a local API and graph scripts on the workstation.

faq.question: Does it require Bash?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill is built around Bash commands for graph queries and indexing.

faq.question: Can it work without an indexed graph?
faq.answer: No. The project must be indexed before dependency queries can return useful results.

faq.question: Does it send code to an external service?
faq.answer: No evidence of external network access was found. The documented API endpoint is localhost.

faq.question: Why review commands before use?
faq.answer: The skill runs PATH-resolved scripts that are not included in the reviewed package.

faq.question: Who benefits most from this skill?
faq.answer: Developers who need dependency context before refactoring or changing shared code benefit most.
